passages.text: But Peter ......... diōtata, God orders our affairs. For we have Annoubion with us .......... ogon. For when we are staying in Antioch, this man will thereafter discuss nativity with us more sincerely, as a friend. And so, when the father set out by night for nearby Antioch with those whom Peter had instructed, together with Annoubion, at dawn the next day, before Peter went out for the discussion, Appion and Athenodorus returned to Laodicea, having sent Simon ahead, and began seeking the father. When Peter learned this, he ordered them to enter. After they had entered and sat down, they asked, “Where is Faustus?” Peter answered, “We do not know. For after coming to you that very evening, he was no longer seen by his own people. Yesterday at dawn Simon also sought him, and since we answered him nothing, I do not know what came over him: he declared himself to be Faustus but was not believed, and, weeping and beating himself, he threatened to kill himself and rushed off as though toward the sea.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ θεὸς τὰ πράγματα ἡμῶν οἰκονομεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: God orders our affairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομεῖ denotes managing or arranging affairs; “orders” preserves that sense without adding an explanation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will thereafter discuss nativity
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of Annoubion and astrological discussion, γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, while τοῦ λοιποῦ means thereafter or henceforth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: more sincerely, as a friend
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνησιώτερον can mean more genuinely, sincerely, or candidly; the comparison concerns the openness expected from a friend.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what came over him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “what seemed good to him,” the phrase idiomatically refers to what entered his mind or prompted his conduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: weeping and beating himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόπτομαι can depict striking oneself as an expression of grief; the bodily image is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rushed off as though toward the sea
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς qualifies the reported direction and does not state that he reached or entered the sea.

source_issues.issue: The nine-dot printed lacuna removes wording after “Peter,” and διώτατα has no secure contextual analysis as a standalone form. The exact gap is retained and the surviving form is transliterated; no restoration has been supplied.
The ten-dot printed lacuna removes wording after Annoubion and leaves the fragment όγον. The exact gap and a transliteration of the surviving fragment are retained; no completion has been supplied.

passages.text: On hearing this, Appion and those with him wailed and beat themselves, saying, “Why did you not receive him?” And just as Athenodorus was about to say to me, “It was Faustus, your father,” Appion forestalled him and said, “We learned from someone that Simon, after finding him, sent him away ............................... the truth, Faustus himself having begged him, because he did not wish to see that his own sons had become Jews. When we heard this, we came for this reason, seeking him. But since he is not here, the person who told us appears to have spoken truthfully. As, therefore, we heard it from him, so we have told you.” But I, Clement, understood Peter’s purpose: he wanted to plant in them the suspicion that he was going to demand the old man from them, so that they would become afraid and flee. I therefore joined in his plan and said to Appion, “Listen, my dearest Appion. We were eager to give him, as our father, the things we regarded as good. But if he himself did not wish to receive them and, on the contrary, was disgusted with us and fled—I will say something rather harsh—we do not care about him either.” When I said this, they left, taking offense as though at cruelty, and (as we learned the next day) of us ......., they set out in Simon’s tracks for Judea.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wailed and beat themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verbs portray loud lamentation and bodily striking in grief, so both actions are retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon, after finding him, sent him away
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξορμάω may be intransitive, “set out,” or causative, “send out.” The preceding αὐτόν supports the causative rendering, though the following lacuna prevents certainty.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to plant in them the suspicion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The image of sowing or planting suspicion is preserved.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς τὸν γέροντα ζητεῖν μέλλων παρ’ αὐτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he was going to demand the old man from them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ζητεῖν παρά may mean to seek information or an accounting from them, or to demand the man from them. “Demand” best explains their anticipated fear, while the alternative remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I therefore joined in his plan
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression literally describes running together with his purpose and contextually means cooperating with or furthering the plan.

lexical_decisions.chosen: was disgusted with us and fled
lexical_decisions.rationale: βδελύσσομαι expresses abhorrence or revulsion, stronger than simple dislike.

lexical_decisions.chosen: taking offense as though at cruelty
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς presents cruelty as their construal of Clement’s words rather than an unqualified judgment by the narrator.

source_issues.issue: The thirty-one-dot printed lacuna removes the construction connecting ἐξώρμησε with τὰ ἀληθῆ. The exact gap is retained, and no missing action or speech has been restored.

The seven-dot printed lacuna removes wording that governed or completed the genitive ἡμῶν. The resulting fragment is preserved in its source order, without conjecturally supplying its syntactic relation.

passages.text: Nevertheless, after ten days had passed, ......... from Antioch, from the father, reporting to us how the father, dēmo........., by denouncing his appearance and speaking well of Peter, had moved the entire city of the Antiochenes into longing. He also reported that, as a result, everyone desired to see him, but that some, angry with him as though he were Simon because of his surpassing affection for Peter, even wanted to lay hands on Faustus as though he were Simon; and that therefore Faustus, fearing that he might be killed, had sent to ask Peter to come immediately, so that Peter might reach him while he was still alive and make a timely appearance before the city while its longing for him was at its height. When Peter heard this, he gathered a great many people for assembly, appointed one of his followers as bishop, baptized and healed, and, after remaining three days in Laodicea, hastened to set out for nearby Antioch.

lexical_decisions.chosen: denouncing his appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ may refer to the father’s present appearance, Simon’s appearance, or the person represented by it. The non-reflexive “his” preserves that referential ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: speaking well of Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this public-speech context εὐλογέω can mean praising or speaking favorably of someone rather than pronouncing a blessing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πᾶσαν Ἀντιοχέων πόλιν εἰς πόθον μετέθηκεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: had moved the entire city of the Antiochenes into longing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source image of transferring or moving the city into a state of longing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: angry with him as though he were Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contextual referent is Faustus under Simon’s appearance, but the pronoun itself does not explicitly name him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὴν πρὸς Πέτρον ὑπερβάλλουσαν στοργὴν
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of his surpassing affection for Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: στοργή denotes strong affection, and ὑπερβάλλουσαν marks it as exceptional or surpassing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐξαυτῆς ἐλθεῖν πέμψαντα ἀξιοῦν· τὸν Πέτρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: had sent to ask Peter to come immediately
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸν Πέτρον is taken as the delayed object of ἀξιοῦν. The editorial punctuation makes the attachment conspicuous but does not prevent this contextually defensible construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that Peter might reach him while he was still alive
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here means to catch up with or reach someone; ζῶντα describes the endangered Faustus.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ πόλει ἀκμαζούσῃ πόθῳ τῷ πρὸς αὐτὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: before the city while its longing for him was at its height
lexical_decisions.rationale: The city is portrayed as being at its peak or flourishing in its longing; the pronoun most naturally refers to Peter but remains formally pronominal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he gathered a great many people for assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκκλησιάζειν can denote convening or addressing an assembly and need not imply a later formalized church service.

lexical_decisions.chosen: appointed one of his followers as bishop
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίσκοπος denotes the appointed overseer; “bishop” preserves the narrative’s office term.

source_issues.issue: The nine-dot printed lacuna removes the main subject and/or verbal wording before the masculine participle ἀγγελῶν. The fragment is retained without inventing a messenger or finite verb.

The nine-dot printed lacuna follows the surviving fragment δημο and removes the remainder of the word or phrase. The fragment is transliterated and the exact gap retained; no adverb such as “publicly” has been restored.
